stem: A 63-year-old man comes to the office due to long-standing osteoarthritis that is refractory to over-the-counter analgesics.  After discussion of treatment options, the patient is referred to a surgeon for right total hip arthroplasty.  His acute postoperative course is unremarkable.  During a follow-up appointment, the patient reports difficulty walking despite minimal pain.  On examination, he leans to his right side when walking.  When the patient is asked to stand on his right leg, his left hip tilts downward.  Which of the following nerves is most likely injured in this patient?​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌​
explanation:
This patient has superior gluteal nerve injury, which is most often caused by pelvic trauma or iatrogenic damage occurring during hip surgery or buttocks injections.  The superior gluteal nerve innervates the gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae muscles.  These muscles stabilize the pelvis and abduct the thigh at the hip.

After nerve injury, weakness of the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus muscles causes the pelvis to sag toward the unaffected (contralateral) side when the patient stands on the affected leg (positive Trendelenburg sign).  When walking, the patient leans toward the affected (ipsilateral) side to compensate for the hip drop (gluteus medius lurch).

(Choice A)  The femoral nerve innervates the muscles responsible for flexion of the thigh at the hip (eg, iliacus and sartorius muscles) and extension of the leg at the knee (eg, quadriceps femoris).  It also supplies sensory innervation to the skin on the anterior thigh and medial leg.  Injury results in knee buckling and loss of the patellar reflex.

(Choice B)  The inferior gluteal nerve innervates the gluteus maximus muscle, which is responsible for extension and external rotation of the thigh at the hip.  Injury typically causes difficulty in rising from a seated position and climbing stairs.

(Choice C)  The obturator nerve innervates the muscles of the medial compartment of the thigh and provides sensory innervation to the medial thigh skin.  Injury causes impaired thigh adduction.

(Choice D)  The sciatic nerve innervates the muscles in the posterior compartment of the thigh (ie, hamstrings).  It subsequently divides into the tibial and common fibular/common peroneal nerves, which provide motor and sensory innervation to the leg and foot.

Educational objective:Superior gluteal nerve injury results in weakness of the gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae muscles.  This causes the pelvis to sag toward the unaffected side (positive Trendelenburg sign).  Patients also lean toward the affected side when walking to help stabilize the pelvis (gluteus medius lurch).​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌​
